summary: Give the Cable impedance calculator the inner diameter of surface shield, the substrate dielectric relative permittivity, the impedance and the capacitance and it returns impedance (Results). Think of it as a shortcut for whatever you happen to be working on. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Cable impedance calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cable impedance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports impedance (Results) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the cable Type); then you type in the inner diameter of surface shield (D), the substrate dielectric relative permittivity, the impedance (Results) and the capacitance (Results).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as coaxial and twisted Pair. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in micrometers. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in ohms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in picofarads per centimeter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in nanohenries per centimeter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cable impedance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Impedance=60 × the natural log of (inner diameter of surface shield (D) ÷ inner conductor diameter (d)) ÷ the square root of (substrate dielectric relative permittivity)
Delay=(1059 ÷ 12500) × the square root of (substrate dielectric relative permittivity)
Inner conductor diameter (d)=inner diameter of surface shield (D) × the exponential of (-25 ÷ 127 × inductance)
Inner conductor diameter (d)=inner diameter of surface shield (D) × the exponential of (-141 ÷ 100 × substrate dielectric relative permittivity ÷ capacitance)
Cutoff frequency=(59 ÷ 2500) ÷ (PI × the square root of (substrate dielectric relative permittivity) × (inner conductor diameter (d) + inner diameter of surface shield (D)))
Separation between wires (S)=(1 ÷ 2) × diameter of the wires (D) × the exponential of ((1 ÷ 120) × impedance × the square root of (substrate dielectric relative permittivity))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in micrometers
  • Length, opening in micrometers
  • Length, opening in micrometers
  • Length, opening in micrometers
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • EEweb capacitance per unit length, opening in picofarads per centimeter
  • EEweb capacitance per unit length, opening in picofarads per centimeter

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cable impedance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the inner diameter of surface shield, the substrate dielectric relative permittivity and the impedance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Cable impedance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns impedance (Results), derived from the inner diameter of surface shield, the substrate dielectric relative permittivity and the impedance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cable impedance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the inner diameter of surface shield, the substrate dielectric relative permittivity, the impedance and the capacitance, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter inner conductor diameter (d) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Inner conductor diameter (d) opens in micrometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Cable impedance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
